extracted.intended_audience: applied mathematicians, computational mathematicians, and researchers using computation as an active research tool
extracted.subtask_description: Principles, practices, and methodological criteria for conducting experimental applied mathematics research — i.e., using computation for exploration, discovery, conjecture-formation, and validation in applied-math problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation for exploration and discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Computation used as an active agent of research for gaining insight and intuition, discovering new patterns and relationships, testing conjectures, and confirming analytically derived results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use computational experiments to suggest phenomena and conjectures (examples: gravitational boosting discovery, fractal/chaos exploration, numeric discovery of the uncertainty principle). Typical workflows include numerical experimentation, perturbation/search strategies (e.g., start with a tent function, perturb on a grid, refine δ until convergence like 10^−6), discretization (e.g., FFT approximations of transforms), and iterative refinement. Use computation to reveal structure that analytic methods may miss or to guide analytic proof attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic computing
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ symbolic computation (CAS) as one of the core toolsets in experimental applied mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage systems such as Maple and Mathematica for symbolic manipulation and some high-precision support; be aware of limitations (performance and correctness issues for some special-function derivatives). Use symbolic tools for exploratory algebra, manipulations that inform numeric work, and to produce expressions amenable to integer-relation searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-precision arithmetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Use arithmetic beyond standard 64-bit (≈16 decimal digits) when required — e.g., double-double/quad-precision (~31 digits), hundreds or thousands of digits for certain studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose precision based on problem sensitivity: unstable periodic orbits, PSLQ/integer-relation searches, and special-function identities often require hundreds to thousands of digits. Tools: Maple, Mathematica (with caveats), GNU multiprecision libraries, specialized high-precision libraries. Be mindful of algorithmic challenges for transcendental functions at very high precision; validate results with independent checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integer relation algorithms (PSLQ/LLL) for discovering identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Given high-precision numerical vectors, apply integer-relation algorithms (commonly PSLQ; LLL can be adapted) to find integer-linear relations among computed constants and thereby conjecture closed-form identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute all candidate terms to sufficiently high precision (often several hundred to thousands of digits), supply vector (x1,x2,...,xn) to PSLQ; the algorithm either finds a relation or provides a lower bound on the Euclidean norm of any relation vector. Use found relations to propose experimental identities (examples: discovering C4 = 7ζ(3)/12, many relations among elliptic integrals). Confirm conjectured identities with higher precision and, where possible, analytic proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphics and visualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use graphics and visualization as exploratory tools to reveal qualitative behavior and patterns (fractals, chimera states, Lorenz attractor, snow crystal morphology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize time-series, phase patterns, attractors, densities, and small-scale zooms to detect structure and guide subsequent quantitative or analytic work. Examples: fractal plots, phase patterns for chimera states, multi-scale zooms on Lorenz attractor to show nontrivial structure. Public simulators (e.g., Snofakes) can aid reproducibility and exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connections with nontraditional mathematics / cross-disciplinary interplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively seek and exploit connections across diverse parts of pure, applied, and computational mathematics and between mathematical fields and applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for interplay between computational tool development (special functions, polylogarithms) and structural discoveries (random-walk measures, Mahler measures, elliptic integral relations). Such cross-connections often lead to new identities and analytic insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate role of rigorous proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance the role of rigorous proof and computational evidence: in some applied contexts formal proof of every minor component is less valuable than strong computational evidence for methods; in others, proof remains essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use computation to provide strong evidence and to guide analytic proofs. Recognize when rigorous proof is necessary for foundational claims and when computational confirmation suffices for practical purposes. Explicitly document whether results are conjectural (numerically observed) or proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity checks and verification practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Routinely insert validity checks in computations that exploit known high-level mathematical facts (e.g., matrix products should give identity, convolution of integer data should be integer-like).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ independent verification methods: cross-check with a different algorithm or implementation, use known identities/invariants, compare to independently computed special positions (e.g., Kanada's hex-digit cross-check of π using BBP vs independent computation). Use multiple series terms or analytic expansions to resolve apparent numerical coincidences (example: apparent π/8 equality that disagreed after 42 digits was resolved by including further series terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of limits of computation and common error sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and plan for many possible sources of computational error: unreliable numerical algorithms, buggy programs, system/compiler/hardware errors, insufficient precision, and obscure large-scale computation bugs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to detect and mitigate these errors: sanity checks, independent reimplementation, increased precision, interval/arbitrary-precision arithmetic where appropriate, and conservative interpretation of surprising results until validated. Document error bounds and validation procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-precision methods for unstable dynamics and periodic orbits
rubrics_metrics.description: Use high-precision numerical integrators for studying highly unstable periodic orbits and chaotic dynamics where low precision leads to loss of digits per period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether initial conditions produce periodic orbits up to a given tolerance; if orbits are highly unstable and lose digits each period, increase precision (double, quadruple, hundred-digit or more) to avoid artifacts (e.g., gaps in plotted families of orbits). Combine methods: Lindstedt-Poincaré perturbation, Newton's method, Fourier interpolation with high-precision libraries to obtain meaningful results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large-scale and parallel computation for deep exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: Use high-performance and parallel computing resources for long, high-precision searches and verification tasks that are infeasible on single-workstation timescales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include multi-hour highly parallel computations to confirm identities to 250-digit precision or PSLQ searches across thousands of integrals at 3200-digit precision. Plan for computational scale, resource allocation, and reproducibility of large runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized numerical methods for special functions and polylogarithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop or use specialized algorithms and libraries for evaluating special functions (Bessel, elliptic integrals, polylogarithms, polylog derivatives) at very high precision, since general-purpose CAS may be slow or inaccurate for these tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that Maple/Mathematica may struggle or be slow for high-precision derivatives of polylog; consider specialized implementations or numerical strategies to compute required values efficiently and reliably. Use these to feed PSLQ and other relation searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental-to-analytic pipeline (conjecture then prove)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use numerical experimentation to conjecture closed forms and relationships, then seek analytic proofs; sometimes experimental discoveries (occasionally from fortunate errors) motivate rigorous results later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat numerical identities as conjectures until proven; use high-precision confirmation (hundreds-to-thousands of digits) to increase confidence, then attempt to locate analytic structures (e.g., zeros of zeta functions, Mahler measures) that explain the numerics. Document provenance: how numerical evidence led to conjecture and what analytic steps (if any) followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and public availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Make simulators, code, and data available when possible to support reproducibility of computational experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish or host simulators and code (example: Snofakes simulator URL), include enough detail on numerical methods, precisions used, parameter choices, and validation checks so others can reproduce results. For large computations, provide logs, seeds for randomization, and checkpointing information where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of experimental numerical evidence for asymptotics and constant identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Use high-precision computations to determine asymptotic constants and coefficients (example: computing the QRS constant c1 to 42 digits and identifying it as the unique zero of a Hurwitz zeta function on an interval).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute numeric sequences at high precision, fit asymptotic expansions, and use numeric root-finding and special-function evaluations to identify constants; then seek analytic characterization when possible. Validate by increasing precision and cross-verifying with analytic properties (e.g., functional equations, zeta-function identities).
